terms.definition: The closed, repeating path a planet follows around the Sun — a slightly squashed ellipse with the Sun at one focus.
terms.function: Shows how forward motion and inward gravity balance into a loop that repeats with no pushing effort.
terms.whereItIs: The thin rings drawn around the Sun in the model.
terms.whyItMatters: Orbits are the pattern behind every year, every moon phase, and every satellite.

terms.definition: The pull that every mass exerts on every other mass; the Sun's gravity is the pull steering each planet's path.
terms.function: Pulls planets toward the Sun at every moment, bending their straight forward motion into a curve.
terms.whereItIs: Shown as the golden tug arrows in the overlay layer.
terms.whyItMatters: Nothing in the solar system travels on straight paths while gravity is at work — gravity is the reason everything loops.

terms.definition: A closed curve shaped like a slightly squashed circle, with two focus points inside; planets orbit with the Sun at one focus.
terms.function: Explains why a planet's distance to the Sun changes smoothly during its year instead of staying constant.
terms.whereItIs: The shape of every ring in the simulator (exaggerated slightly for Earth's ring).
terms.whyItMatters: Comets' wildly stretched ellipses show how this same shape — not orbit size — is the rule for everything orbiting the Sun.

terms.definition: A ring of millions of small rocky bodies orbiting the Sun between Mars and Jupiter.
terms.function: Marks the boundary between the inner rocky planets and the outer giant planets.
terms.whereItIs: The scattered ring of small spheres between Mars's ring and Jupiter's ring in the model.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the leftover building material from the solar system's formation, and it sits in the largest gap between the planets.

terms.definition: The time a body takes to complete one full orbit around the Sun — one year on that body.
terms.function: Explains why planet cards list different year lengths: the farther out, the wider the loop and the slower the drift, so the period grows.
terms.whereItIs: The clock readout near each ring while the simulator runs.
terms.whyItMatters: The orbital period is the very definition of a planet's year, and it encodes how far that world really is from the Sun.
